name: Treating pain in sickle cell disease by means of focused ultrasound neuromodulation
description: Researchers will develop a novel transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS) device for pain treatment and establish its effectiveness for treating sickle cell disease (SCD) pain in humanized mice. The tFUS will target the specific cortical regions involved in SCD pain using a novel non-invasive electrophysiological source imaging technique. The projects goals have several aims. Aim 1: Develop tFUS devices for pain treatment. The mouse-scale system will be designed to validate the therapeutic effect of stimulating the anticipated cortical targets. This will inform development of the simpler human-scale system, which will use models of the skull to select cost-effective transducers to reach the targets. Aim 2: Evaluate tFUS effectiveness and optimize stimulation parameters in an SCD mice model. Researchers will determine effective tFUS parameters to chronically reduce SCD pain in mice and validate this using behavioral measures. Aim 3: Use electrophysiological source imaging to target and trigger closed-loop tFUS in animal models. This aim also includes performing safety studies to prepare for human trials. The project will develop a transformative, noninvasive tFUS device to effectively and safely treat pain in SCD.

name: Treating pain in sickle cell disease by means of focused ultrasound neuromodulation (Behavior assessments and analyses)
description: We have demonstrated a novel transcranial focused ultrasound technology for pain treatment, that promises to provide non-pharmacologic chronic pain treatment for patients associated with underlying conditions such as cancer or sickle cell disease (SCD). The behavioral assessment with analysis were conducted from 114 experimental in vivo mice.

README

This readme document describes the organized behavior assessment with analysis. This work was supported

in part by NIH EB029354, NS124564, and NS131069. Animal care and handling are according to the

regulation of Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Carnegie Mellon University and Long Beach

VA medical Centre and complied with National Institutes of Health guidelines. If anyone uses the whole or

part of the dataset provided here, we kindly ask you to cite the following publication in any of your

publications or presentations:

Kim MG*, Yu K*, Yeh C-Y, Fouda R, Argueta D, Kiven S, Ni Y, Niu X, Chen Q, Kim K, Gupta K, He B.

Low-intensity transcranial focused ultrasound changes pain-associated behaviors by modulating pain

processing brain circuits. bioRxiv: https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.12.07.519518 (*Equal contribution, first

author)

The animal behavioral assessment with analysis is provided as service to the scientific community and may

be used for any non-commercial purpose.

The folder contains behavioral assessment along with analysis. All behavioral experiments are conducted

during the light cycle of the animals and recorded on video for further validation. For heat hyperalgesia,

the temperature of the hot-plate (Ugo Basile, PA, USA) is pre-determined at 52 °C for sickle (HbSS-BERK)

mice, and hind paw withdrawal latency (hPWL) is determined through blind assessments. For cold

hyperalgesia, the temperature of the cold-plate (Ugo Basile, PA, USA) is pre-determined at 4 °C, and hind

paw withdrawal frequency (hPWF) over a 2-minute period was blindly assessed. For mechanical

hyperalgesia, the minimum threshold of von Frey filaments (Stoelting Co, IL, USA) is calculated using the

up-down method and represented as a hind paw withdrawal threshold (hPWT). Motor performance is

assessed using a rotating rod (Ugo Basile, PA, USA) programmed to gradually increase revolutions per

minute (rpm) from 3 to 72 rpm over 5-min. The integral of time spent on the rod (i.e., latency to fall) is

measured. In the behavioral analysis, the unilateral effect of transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS) is

assessed, and behavioral responses to the hot, cold, and mechanical stimuli are calculated using the

following metrics: ∆ hPWL (s) = contralateral (right) hPWL- ipsilateral (left) hPWL, ∆ hPWF =

contralateral hPWF- ipsilateral hPWF, and ∆ hPWT = contralateral hPWT- ipsilateral hPWT. The number

of example data (n = 8-11 mice) has been provided and the effect of tFUS on different noxious heat, cold,

and mechanical stimuli, ultrasound pulse repetition frequencies (PRF), duty cycle, gender, age, genotype,

head-fixed awake model, and inter-experiment intervals has been investigated (see details in Methods).

Folders:

- Hot-plate test blind assessment and summary

- Cold-plate test blind assessment and summary

- von Frey test blind assessment and summary

- Rotarod test blind assessment and summary

name: Transcranial focused ultrasound neuromodulation on a nonhuman primate model
description: In these datasets, we applied low-intensity tFUS stimulation with a customized 128-element random array ultrasound transducer (f0: 700 kHz) in a rhesus macaque monkey engaged in a simple visually-guided saccade task. The stimulation was guided stereotaxically to the frontal eye field (FEF), a region of frontal cortex that guides eye movements. We recorded simultaneously from a 96-channel Utah array implanted in V4, a region of extrastriate visual cortex that receives feedback connections from FEF.

name: README: tFUS neuromodulation on a nonhuman primate model
README.pdf
content:
Each neural electrophysiological dataset (Ripple Trellis) consists of three

data files, i.e., .ns2, .ns5, and .nev.

To load the local field potentials (LFPs), one can use an software toolbox,

such as Fieldtrip (FieldTrip toolbox), to read the header and data from

the .ns2 file, and read the trigger events from the .nev file.

To load the spiking activities, one can use any eligible toolbox to read the

spike, header, and event information from .nev file. The spike data have been

pre-sorted, and can be further sorted by offline sorter, mksort, Kilosort, etc.

The trigger code for the visual stimulus is 10, and 130 for the ultrasound

stimulus.

Once the trigger events being identified, one can create trial structures to

group the trials with sole visual stimulation, hybrid stimulation (visual+tFUS

stimulation), or sole ultrasound stimulation (for Fig. 5).

After the trials structures being established, one can further do LFP

averaging across multiple trials in each experimental condition, and

implement statistical analyses in the temporal/spatial domain. One can also

pursue the spike timing analyses to generate the peri-stimulus time

histogram, raster plot, etc. The spiking rates can be therefore calculated at

individual time point in each trial.
